title: Vector Semantics
oneLiner: How computers capture word meaning as lists of numbers, by looking at which words keep each other company.

what.html:
Computers need numbers, so we turn each word into a vector (a list of numbers). The trick: a word's meaning shows up in the words around it. Count which words appear near each word (or in which documents), and words with similar meanings end up with similar lists. Then "similar meaning" becomes "pointing in a similar direction".

Everyday versionYou can guess what an unfamiliar dish is from the menu around it: if it's cooked with garlic, served over rice and described by its leaves, it's probably a leafy green.

why.html:
• Search, recommendation, chatbots and translation all need word meaning as numbers.
  • Similar words get similar vectors, so models generalise to words they've rarely seen.
  • It's the basis for Word2Vec, language models and Transformers.

how.title: Words have senses
how.html: A dictionary word (lemma) like "mouse" can have several senses (animal, computer device). A question answerer must also know "tall" relates to "height".

how.title: How words relate
how.html: Same meaning (couch/sofa), alike (coffee/tea), associated (coffee/cup), opposite (hot/cold), kind-of (dog is an animal), part-of (wheel of a car).

how.title: Feelings attached to words
how.html: "Cheap" and "inexpensive" both mean low cost, but feel different. Emotional meaning is often described by pleasantness, intensity and sense of control.

how.title: Judge a word by its company
how.html: Words that appear in similar contexts tend to mean similar things. That single idea lets computers learn meaning from raw text.

how.title: Count the company
how.html: Make a table: rows are words, columns are documents (or nearby words), cells are counts. "battle" shows up in history plays, "fool" in comedies; "cherry" near "pie", "digital" near "computer".

how.title: Compare directions, not sizes
how.html: Frequent words have huge counts everywhere, so a plain dot product overrates them. Cosine similarity compares only the direction: digital/information 0.996, cherry/information 0.019.

how.title: Weight what's informative
how.html: TF-IDF shrinks huge counts with a log and boosts words that appear in only a few documents. A word in every document gets weight 0.

how.title: Short, learned vectors
how.html: Instead of 50,000 sparse counts, learn 50–300 dense numbers per word by predicting neighbours from raw text, labels for free. Looking a word up is just picking its row from a big table.

demo.html: Six tiny sentences about pets and stock markets, turned into 2 numbers per word. Click a word: its neighbours come from the same topic, learned purely from which words appeared together.

example.html:
Why cosine, not dot product. "information" is very frequent, so its dot product with "cherry" (44,443) beats cherry with strawberry (27,004), which is clearly wrong. Dividing by the vectors' lengths gives cosines of 0.019 and 0.969: strawberry wins easily.

Supplementary Opposites like hot/cold appear in the same contexts, so simple word vectors often think they're similar.

misunderstandings: A bigger dot product means more similar words.
It also rewards frequency; use cosine.
Coffee and cup are related, not similar.
takeaways: Lemmas have senses; words relate in several distinct ways.
Term-document and term-term count matrices give sparse vectors.
Cosine fixes the dot product's frequency bias; TF-IDF/PMI reweight counts.
Dense embeddings are learned by self-supervised prediction.
thirty: Lexical semantics studies word meaning: lemmas have senses (polysemy), and words relate by synonymy, similarity, relatedness, antonymy, hypernymy and meronymy; connotation adds affective meaning (valence, arousal, dominance). The distributional hypothesis (words in similar contexts have similar meanings) underlies vector semantics. Count-based vectors come from term-document matrices (battle = [1, 0, 7, 13]) or term-term co-occurrence matrices (cherry, digital, …) and are long and sparse. Cosine similarity normalises the dot product's bias toward frequent words (digital/information 0.996 vs cherry/information 0.019). TF-IDF (tf = log(count + 1), idf = log(N/df)) and PMI reweight counts. Dense 50–300-dimensional embeddings are learned by self-supervised prediction, and an embedding lookup selects a row of the V × D matrix.
